sections.h2: How quickly can a York Township house sell?
sections.html:
A fair price and tidy paperwork make for a quick sale. The township is a big suburb next to the City of York, and buyers keep coming. What you give up in time and in price depends on whether you list with an agent, sell it yourself or take a direct cash offer.

The township has 31,479 residents, up 5.8 percent from a 2020 count of 29,748, and 12,939 households. Owners occupy 70.1 percent of homes. About 22.5 percent of residents are 65 or older, so downsizing and estate sales are common. Demand is healthy, but a house carrying liens, tenants or postponed repairs tends to sit longer than a clean one.

Owner-occupied homes have a midpoint value of $260,800. Monthly housing costs at the midpoint run $1,914 with a mortgage and $768 without, and renters pay $1,389. Household income at the midpoint is $80,190. One township figure covers a lot of ground: a dated ranch and a remodeled house in a newer plan will sell far apart.

Closed sales of similar houses near you, and an appraiser's view, will tell you more than any township average.

sections.h2: Permits and inspections that can affect a sale
sections.html:
Permits, code enforcement and property maintenance all run through the township's Building and Zoning Department. It enforces the statewide Uniform Construction Code, which the township adopted through Ordinance 2004-7 on May 11, 2004. If a finished basement, deck or shed went up without a permit, a buyer's inspector or lender might find it, so look at your file before you list.

  • Residential building permits get up to 15 business days of plan review, commercial ones up to 30.
  • A zoning permit is due in 10 days, unless a special exception or variance must go before the Zoning Hearing Board.
  • Building inspections are booked on weekdays between 7:30 a.m. and 2:15 p.m. with a day's notice, by calling (717) 428-5641.
  • Plumbing work falls under York Township Resolution 93-2. Swapping a fixture or a water heater on the same fuel needs no permit.
  • A home business registers every year for $25.

Call (717) 741-3861 on weekdays until 4:00 p.m. to reach zoning and code staff, and book an appointment before you visit. Ask also about the LERTA tax assistance program for certain deteriorated areas if your parcel could qualify.

sections.h2: Recording the deed and transfer tax
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded by the York County Recorder of Deeds, not by the township. Its fees are modest but itemized.

York County recording fees
Recording itemFee
Deed, base fee (four pages, four names)$86.25
Each page past the fourth$2
Each additional name$0.50
Each parcel identification number on the paper$20
Realty Transfer Tax Statement of Value$2
Returned check$50

The office takes business checks, personal checks and cash. The state's transfer tax is 1 percent of value, owed jointly by buyer and seller, with municipal and school shares possibly added on top. Your title company or the recorder can give the total for your deed. Certain family gifts and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt.

There are three common ways to sell.

  • Agent listing. A listing gets the most eyes on the house and suits one in good order. The costs are a commission, showings and a wait on the buyer's loan, appraisal and inspection.
  • Owner sale. Selling yourself saves the commission, but pricing, marketing, contracts and haggling are yours. Transfer tax and recording costs stay.
  • Cash offer. A direct buyer purchases the house as it stands, so cleanouts, repairs and tenants are less of an obstacle. The price usually comes in under a fully prepared retail sale, which is why you should compare it with a listing's net after commission and fix-up.

Inherited homes, stubborn tenants, long-postponed repairs and hard deadlines such as a job relocation all point toward cash. Get a written offer for your address, then lay it next to a listing estimate.

Pull the deed and the newest tax bill, along with permit records for any work on the house. Every mortgage or lien needs a payoff statement, since you pay them out of the sale proceeds. If a relative left you the house, line up the estate papers that show who can sign.

Next, tour the house as an inspector would, checking the roof, furnace, electrical panel, sump area and outbuildings and noting work done without a permit. Then pick: repair, give a credit, or sell as-is. With a repair estimate in hand, listing versus direct offer is simple math.

sections.h2: Houses with tenants, liens or inherited title
sections.html:
These are the situations that slow an open-market sale the most. Tenants in place restrict showings and can complicate a closing date. Liens come out of your proceeds, so learn the payoff early. Inherited houses require clear proof of who may sign. None of these blocks a sale, but each adds steps, and a direct buyer who accepts the house as-is can often handle them in a single closing.

Whichever route you pick, put in writing who pays for cleanout, back taxes and recording. Surprises at the settlement table usually come from items nobody assigned.

• What is the closing date, and can it move if title work runs long?
  • Does the offer depend on a loan, an appraisal or an inspection?
  • Who covers recording fees and the transfer tax share?
  • If the house has unpermitted work, will the buyer take it as it stands?

Written answers let you compare a cash offer and a financed offer on the same terms, and they protect you if the buyer changes course later.

1. Phone the Building and Zoning Department at (717) 741-3861 and ask what the file shows for your parcel.
  2. Request a payoff letter from each lender.
  3. Locate the deed and confirm every name on it matches the people who will sign.
  4. Photograph the roof line, furnace, panel and sump area so you can answer buyer questions without guessing.
  5. Collect two or three written offers, one of them a direct cash offer, and rank them by net proceeds and closing date.

That short list prevents most delays. When something does turn up late, an unpermitted shed or a forgotten lien, you will already know whom to call.

After you accept an offer, call the Building and Zoning Department about anything unpermitted, and order payoff statements. The title company drafts the deed and checks the transfer tax and recording fees. At settlement you sign, the tax is paid and the deed goes to the York County Recorder of Deeds. A financed buyer adds a lender appraisal and inspection, which is why listed houses commonly take weeks to a few months. A cash buyer can close faster, and you often choose the date.

faqs.q: What is the typical timeline to sell in York Township?
faqs.a: Listed houses commonly take weeks to a few months depending on price, condition and the buyer's loan. A cash sale can close sooner because no lender or appraisal is involved, and the seller often sets the closing date.

faqs.q: Is a permit required before selling a York Township house?
faqs.a: No permit is needed just to sell. Earlier unpermitted work is the concern, because a buyer's inspection can raise it. Call the Building and Zoning Department at (717) 741-3861 to ask what the township file shows.

faqs.q: Which office records the deed for a York Township sale?
faqs.a: The York County Recorder of Deeds. The base fee for a deed is $86.25 for four pages and four names, plus charges for added pages, names and parcel numbers.

faqs.q: Who owes Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax?
faqs.a: Buyer and seller are both liable. The state takes 1 percent of the value, and local shares can be added. Your sales agreement sets who pays what.

faqs.q: Can a house that needs repairs still be sold here?
faqs.a: Yes. A direct buyer takes it in its current condition, while a financed buyer tends to ask for repairs or a lower price after inspection. A repair estimate up front lets you compare what each path would net.
